bhāradvāja.notes: DN 13 names both Tārukkha’s pupil (5.1–5.2) and the ancient seer (13.1). MN 95 even uses the name for Kāpaṭika and the seer in the same segment (13.9). Neither discourse can take a single identification. Entry 05 surveys the clan and mentions the seer in passing. Bare addresses and ordination formulas often denote individual members, including Saṅgārava in MN 100 and Piṇḍola in SN 35.127. DPD’s fifth sense points to Sundarika in MN 7 and to the elder who rejoices at his son’s liberation in Thag 2.29. Neither passage identifies Dhanañjānī’s husband of SN 7.1 (03). MN 75 identifies the owner of the fire chamber (06), while its citation also lands on MN 74. The MN 99 citation for 04 reaches a list of seers. Entry 05 calls Kasi a lay disciple, as in SN 7.11, while Snp 1.4 ends with his ordination and arahantship.

bhāvitatta.notes: The entry counts two privately awakened Buddhas. MN 116 names Bhāvitatta after Sutavā in the prose list (4.12–4.13) and repeats the same sequence in verse (5.8). These passages establish one bearer of the name.

bilaṅgikabhāradvāja.notes: SN 7.4 names Bilaṅgika and describes his angry silence. The same page citation also reaches Asurindaka in SN 7.3 and Ahiṁsaka in SN 7.5.

bimbisāra.notes: MN 14:20 names King Seniya Bimbisāra in the discussion of pleasure. Check DPD’s MN 13 hint and the extra MN 15 page match. Thag 1.64 refers to the father by his banner, which explains the citation without a tap on Bimbisāra.

bimbī.notes: The list of laywomen in AN 8.91–117 names Bimbī. The page citation also reaches AN 8.89 and 8.90, both about monastic discipline.

bodhi.notes: MN 85 names the prince and his Kokanada palace. The page also reaches MN 86. MN 116:6.25 names the privately awakened Buddha, for whom the packet has no entry. Bodhiṁ in MN 26:25.1 and MN 85:49.2 refers to Bodhgaya, and Thig 15.1:5.4 addresses the nun Bodhī. The packet misses the chapter summary at MN 90:19.3, where Bodhi refers back to the prince’s discourse.

brahmadatta.notes: DN 14 explicitly names Kassapa’s brahmin father. The packet lacks entries for him and for the king in DPD’s Jātaka example. Thag 6.14:7.7 lists the elder of Thag 6.12 in the chapter summary.

brahmadeva.notes: SN 6.3 tells the episode of the monk visiting his mother. SN 6.2 is an adjacent page match. The name in SN 6.10:11.1 recaps SN 6.3.

brahmāyu.notes: MN 91 introduces the 120-year-old brahmin of Mithilā and his pupil Uttara. The page also lands on MN 90. The packet misses Brahmāyu in the chapter summary at MN 100:44.1.

bāhiya.notes: AN 1.216 names Dārucīriya in the swift-insight list. AN 4.243 names Anuruddha’s pupil. SN 35.89 gives Bāhiya the teaching on the impermanence of the senses, and SN 35.93:4.2 recaps that discourse. SN 47.15 gives a Bāhiya the four establishments of mindfulness, and SN 47.20:4.2 recaps it. Entry 03 itself calls the identification of these two monks tentative, so the SN 47 passages have no pick. The citation ranges also reach AN 1.198–208, AN 1.219–234, AN 4.242, SN 35.88 and SN 47.14.

bāhuraggi.notes: SN 1.50 and SN 2.24 both have Pali bāhuraggi among the seven freed in Aviha. Sujato renders the name Bāhudanti and Bāhudantī respectively. The citation also lands on SN 1.49 and misses the parallel in SN 2.24.

bārāṇasī.notes: AN 3.15 opens at Isipatana near Bārāṇasī. The page also reaches AN 3.14. Check the entry’s inclusion of Kapilavatthu among the four pilgrimage places. DN 16:5.8.3 specifies the Buddha’s birthplace, which Snp 3.11:5.3 locates at Lumbinī.

campā.notes: AN 7.52 and SN 8.11 open at Gaggarā’s lotus pond in Campā. The citation pages also reach AN 7.51 and SN 8.10.
